988.title: Ladino
988.hook: Judeo-Spanish, the language of the Sephardi diaspora
988.howItsDone: Sephardi families and synagogues keep Ladino alive in songs, proverbs and some prayers and readings, and today there are classes, choirs and recordings devoted to it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mizrahi, and your line: the east. A word that depends on where you stand. Today a new week begins, with a language that traveled from the far west of Europe toward the east.

A grandmother in Istanbul tucks a child into bed and sings a lullaby. The words are Spanish, almost. Someone from Madrid would catch half of it and stumble on the rest. Hebrew words are woven through it, and Turkish ones, and on an old printed page the whole song might be spelled in Hebrew letters. That lullaby came a very long way to reach that bedroom, in people's mouths, not in a suitcase. Today's word is the name of the language it's sung in: Ladino.
screen: `A LULLABY IN ISTANBUL.` → `SPANISH, ALMOST.` → `IN HEBREW LETTERS.`

segments.voice: Ladino is Judeo-Spanish: the Spanish that Jews carried with them when they were expelled from Spain, and kept speaking, generation after generation, far from Spain. Families settled across the Ottoman lands, in cities like Salonika, Istanbul, Izmir and Sarajevo, and the language went with them. Start with the name of the people who spoke it. The prophet Obadiah, in a single verse, speaks of exiles of Jerusalem living in a place called Sepharad. Nobody can say for sure what place Obadiah meant. But Jewish tradition came to read Sepharad as Spain. So the Jews of Spain became Sephardim, the people of Sepharad, and Ladino became the language of the Sephardi diaspora. Now the language itself. Back in Spain, Spanish kept changing. Ladino went its own way. Speakers of modern Spanish sometimes say it sounds like an older book come to life. And it picked up new neighbors' words as it went: Hebrew for holy things, Turkish and Greek and others for the market and the street. A few words to taste. Kerido, or kerida: dear. Ke haber? What's new? A psalm asks how anyone can sing the Lord's song in a foreign land. Ladino is one people's answer: you sing it in the language you carried. Ballads, proverbs, wedding songs, lullabies and prayers for home, passed from grandmother to grandchild. Today far fewer families speak Ladino at home, and teachers, singers and writers are working to keep it in the world. Every song they keep is a little bit of Sepharad, still traveling.

989.title: New Amsterdam, 1654
989.hook: Jewish refugees from Brazil come ashore at a Dutch town and ask to stay
989.howItsDone: Jewish communities keep funds and volunteers to care for their own poor and for newcomers, and Congregation Shearith Israel in New York tells the story of the Brazil refugees as its beginning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ladino, and your line: judeo-spanish. A language carried in people's mouths. Today the road crosses an ocean, and a new stretch begins: the Americas.

A small ship comes into a harbor at the tip of an island. On shore there's a Dutch trading town: a fort, a wall, a few streets, and a governor who doesn't want the people on board. They are Jewish men, women and children who have fled Brazil, where they had lived under Dutch rule until the Portuguese took the colony back. They have very little left. The town is New Amsterdam. Today's word is its name, the name it carried before it became New York.
screen: `A SHIP AT THE TIP OF AN ISLAND.` → `REFUGEES FROM BRAZIL.` → `A GOVERNOR WHO SAYS NO.`

segments.voice: The story is handed down with a number, the one in today's line: twenty-three arrived. Families, not soldiers or merchants with full purses. The governor, Peter Stuyvesant, wrote to his employers in Amsterdam, the Dutch West India Company, asking to send them away. But in Amsterdam, Jewish merchants had a stake in the company, and they wrote too, asking that the refugees be allowed to stay. The company's answer came with a condition. The Jews could live and trade in New Amsterdam, as long as their poor did not become a burden on the town or the company. Their own community would care for them. It sounds like a door held half open. But the condition asked for something the Torah already asks. When someone among you is in need, Deuteronomy says, "thou shalt not harden thy heart, nor shut thy hand from thy needy brother." The company meant it as a limit. The community heard a commandment it already kept. And the newcomers kept pushing the door wider. One of them, Asser Levy, is remembered for asking to stand guard on the town watch like any other resident, instead of paying a tax to be excused. Others asked for land to bury their dead. Out of these small requests grew a congregation, Shearith Israel, which still traces its beginning to those arrivals. Its name is Hebrew for the remnant of Israel: what's left, still standing. Twenty-three people, a refusal, a condition, and then a guard post, a burial ground and a congregation.

990.title: A letter to Newport (1790)
990.hook: to the Newport congregation, the government gives "to bigotry no sanction"
990.howItsDone: In Newport the president's letter is read aloud at a yearly public gathering at the old synagogue, and its phrase about bigotry is quoted when people speak about religious freedom in the United States.

segments.voice: Yesterday, New Amsterdam, and your line: twenty-three arrived. Refugees who kept pushing the door wider. Today, a later chapter in the same young country, told in two letters.

A small congregation in Newport, Rhode Island, hears that the president of the new United States is coming to town. Their warden, Moses Seixas, sits down to write a welcome on their behalf, and he chooses his words with care. Jews had lived under rulers who allowed them in one year and turned on them the next, so he writes about what kind of government this new one is. The president writes back. And when the reply arrives, Seixas's own phrase is in it.
screen: `A WELCOME FROM NEWPORT.` → `A WARDEN CHOOSES HIS WORDS.` → `THE PRESIDENT WRITES BACK.`

segments.voice: Seixas described the new government as one that gives no approval to bigotry and no help to persecution. In the reply, the president took that phrase and gave it back as a promise: "For happily the Government of the United States, which gives to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance, requires only that they who live under its protection should demean themselves as good citizens." Notice what happened. The line people quote from this letter was first written by a Jewish warden in Newport. The president heard it, and signed his name under it. Then the letter goes a step further. It says the time is past when people speak of toleration, as if one group's rights were a favor granted by another. Toleration means, we put up with you. The letter says these rights belong to you already. They aren't a gift. Near the end, the letter reaches for the Hebrew prophets. It hopes the children of Abraham in this land will keep the good will of their neighbors, while everyone sits in safety under his own vine and fig tree, with none to make him afraid. That's the prophet Micah's picture of peace: "And none shall make them afraid." A congregation's welcome, a phrase handed back, and a verse from Micah: the letter is all three. It didn't end bigotry. Jews in America would still meet plenty of it. But it gave them a sentence, from the top of the government, to hold the country to.

991.title: The great wave (1881–1924)
991.hook: Jewish families cross from Eastern Europe to America, fleeing poverty and pogroms
991.carry: a bundle and a folded ticket
991.howItsDone: Some Jewish families keep the stories, ship records and photographs of the ancestors who crossed, and at the Passover seder the Haggadah reads and explains the verse about the wandering Aramean.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the letter to Newport, and your line: no sanction to bigotry. Rights, not favors. Today, the door that letter described gets very crowded.

A steamship ticket, folded so many times the creases have gone soft. It arrives in an envelope from America, in a small town in the Russian Empire. The one who sent it left alone, months or years ago, worked in a shop, slept in a crowded room, saved coins in a jar, and bought passage for the next person in the family. Now that person packs a bundle, says goodbye at the edge of town, and goes. Then they save for the next ticket. Today's word is what all those tickets added up to.
screen: `A TICKET IN AN ENVELOPE.` → `ONE WENT FIRST.` → `NOW THE NEXT ONE GOES.`

segments.voice: In the years in today's title, Jews from Eastern Europe crossed to America in a great wave: from the Russian Empire, from Galicia in Austria-Hungary, from Romania and beyond. Two things pushed them. The first was poverty. Under the tsars, Jews were held to certain regions and shut out of many trades and schools, and the towns were crowded and poor. The second was the pogroms: mob attacks on Jewish neighborhoods, homes and shops looted, people beaten and killed, while the authorities often did little to stop them. So families worked out a plan. One goes first, then sends a ticket back. They crossed land to the ports, then the ocean, packed below deck, and came through the inspection halls at the harbor. In Yiddish, some called America di goldene medine, the golden land. The streets were not paved with gold. But there were no pogroms, and a child could go to school. The Torah has words for this kind of family story. When a farmer brought the first fruits to the Temple, he said a short history aloud, starting: "A wandering Aramean was my father." My ancestor wandered, went down to Egypt, lived there as a stranger, and became a people. The Passover Haggadah reads and explains that verse every year. A wanderer, a journey, a stranger who becomes a people: the great wave lived that sentence again. The years in the title end when new American laws sharply narrowed the door. By then whole neighborhoods, synagogues and newspapers had been built by people who arrived with a bundle and a folded ticket.

segments.voice: Think of your ancestors, as far back as you can go, whatever their faith or country: somebody made a journey, or stayed when leaving would have been easier. If you know the story, walk it in your mind; if not, sit with the people whose names are lost but whose choices made you, and if you pray, remember them in prayer.

992.title: Emma Lazarus
992.hook: her poem on the Statue of Liberty welcomes the tired and the poor
992.howItsDone: Jewish communities and teachers sometimes read Emma Lazarus's sonnet beside the Torah's command about the stranger, and Jewish refugee and immigrant aid groups draw on both.

segments.voice: Yesterday, goldene medine, and your line: a bundle and a folded ticket. America, one saved ticket at a time. Today, a poet who watched that wave arriving, and wrote it a welcome.

"Give me your tired, your poor." Those words hang on a plaque at the Statue of Liberty. They weren't there when the statue went up. A young poet in New York wrote them for a fundraiser, to help pay for the statue's pedestal. After the fundraiser, the poem was set aside. She died before anyone put it on the plaque. Today, the woman who gave a silent statue its voice. Her name was Emma Lazarus.
screen: `GIVE ME YOUR TIRED, YOUR POOR.` → `A POEM FOR A PEDESTAL.` → `PUT UP AFTER SHE WAS GONE.`

segments.voice: Emma Lazarus did not come over in the great wave. She came from a Sephardi family long settled in New York, comfortable and educated, with roots in the congregation from three days ago, the one that traces its beginning to the refugees from Brazil. She read widely and wrote poems from a young age. Then refugees from the pogroms began arriving at the docks. She is remembered for going to meet them, working with the newcomers, and writing about Jewish life and Jewish dignity with a new fire. Then came the poem, a sonnet called "The New Colossus." The old Colossus was a giant bronze statue of the ancient Greek world. Her poem opens with what the new statue is not: "Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame, With conquering limbs astride from land to land." Instead, a woman with a torch stands at the gate, and her name is "Mother of Exiles." A giant built for welcome instead of conquest. Then the statue speaks, with silent lips: "Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free." The Torah gives a reason for that kind of welcome, a reason from memory: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt." You've been the stranger, so you know how it feels from the inside. A Jewish poet from an old family looked at strangers stepping off the boat with nothing, and wrote words that let the statue say: I know your heart. Come in.

993.title: The Lower East Side
993.howItsDone: Jewish families, museums and synagogues on the Lower East Side keep the tenement stories, and Psalm 128 is sung or read in Jewish life, including in some communities at weddings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emma Lazarus, and your line: the new colossus. A statue built for welcome. Today, past the statue and the inspection halls, to the streets where newcomers went next.

Five flights of narrow stairs. At the top, a small apartment: a kitchen, a front room, and a dark room in between with no window at all. In the front room a sewing machine is already running before sunrise, because the family is paid by the piece. A boarder sleeps on two chairs pushed together. Down in the street, pushcarts sell herring, pickles, pots and eyeglasses. And a few blocks away, tonight, a theater will fill with people laughing and weeping in Yiddish. Today, the Lower East Side.
screen: `FIVE FLIGHTS UP.` → `A SEWING MACHINE BEFORE SUNRISE.` → `PUSHCARTS AND A YIDDISH THEATER.`

segments.voice: The Lower East Side is a neighborhood in Manhattan, and for the Jewish families of the great wave it was often the first address in America, shared with Italian, Irish and other immigrant neighbors. Start with the tenements: apartment buildings packed tight, room after room, with little light or air. Toilets were in the hall or the yard. Families took in boarders to make the rent. Over time, reformers pushed for laws that required windows, light and better plumbing, because the buildings themselves were making people sick. Then the work. A great deal of it was in the garment trade: cutting, sewing, pressing, in small crowded shops called sweatshops, or at the kitchen table, paid by the piece. Long days, low pay, and the boss could always find someone newer and hungrier. And yet the same streets were full of life. Yiddish newspapers, with letters from readers asking for advice about love, work and faith. Synagogues in storefronts and in grand buildings. Cafés full of arguments. And the Yiddish theater, where tired workers paid a little to watch family dramas, comedies, even Shakespeare in Yiddish, and wept openly in their seats. A psalm holds up the picture these families were working toward: "When thou eatest the labour of thy hands, happy shalt thou be, and it shall be well with thee." Not riches. Just eating from your own work, and having it be enough. In the tenements, the labor was brutal and the bread was thin. But people kept singing, praying and going to the theater, and their children climbed down those five flights to school.

segments.voice: Look at one thing near you, your shirt, your chair, your food, and follow it back: someone sewed it, built it, picked it, packed it. Let one of those unseen workers become real in your mind, tired hands and a long shift, and hold them for a few breaths with respect.

Your line: the tenements. Less room, less light, and still a whole life. Day nine hundred ninety-three.

994.title: The Triangle fire (1911)
994.hook: a fire in a garment factory takes young immigrant workers' lives, and labor laws follow
994.howItsDone: Each year in New York the Triangle fire is remembered at the site, where the workers' names are read aloud, and Jewish labor groups and synagogues have joined in marking the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, pushcarts, and your line: the tenements. Crowded rooms, hard work, and a life anyway. Today ends the week, with one afternoon from those same streets that changed the law.

Late on a Saturday afternoon, near quitting time, on the top floors of a building in Manhattan. Rows of sewing machines. Young women bent over shirtwaists, the blouses of the day, with scraps of cotton piled under the tables. Someone shouts that there's a fire. The scraps catch like paper. Workers run for the stairs, the elevator, the doors. And one of the doors won't open. It's locked. Today's word is the name of that factory, and of that afternoon: the Triangle fire.
screen: `NEAR QUITTING TIME.` → `SCRAPS CATCH LIKE PAPER.` → `ONE DOOR IS LOCKED.`

segments.voice: The Triangle Waist Company made shirtwaists, and the people who sewed them were immigrants, among them young Jewish and Italian women from the streets of yesterday. Doors were kept locked, it was said, to stop workers from slipping out or taking things. When the fire came, a locked door, a collapsing fire escape and ladders that couldn't reach high enough left workers trapped. Some died inside. Some jumped. Crowds in the street watched it happen. This lesson stays there only as long as it takes to honor them. Then the city mourned. Mourners marched in the rain behind the coffins of the unclaimed dead. A young labor organizer, Rose Schneiderman, stood up at a public meeting and told the city it had failed these workers, and that working people would have to save themselves. And something did change. New York set up an investigation that went factory to factory, and new laws followed: fire exits and drills, sprinklers, and limits on hours. The Torah has a line that sits right under this story: "Neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." Not just: don't harm. Don't stand by when someone else is in danger. The same chapter says a worker's wages must not sit with you overnight. Remembering the workers means asking who is behind the locked door today. And this whole week has been about newcomers: a language carried from Spain, refugees at New Amsterdam, a letter, a great wave, a poet, a neighborhood, and today, a fire that rewrote the rules.
screen: `A LOCKED DOOR.` · `THE CITY MOURNS.` · `NEW LAWS FOR SAFER WORK.` · `DO NOT STAND IDLY BY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE WORKERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the workers of that afternoon, young women and men who came for a better life, and hold them in silence for a few breaths; if you pray, remember them in prayer. Then think of one worker in your own world today whose safety or pay is easy to overlook.
